b:
Distributed systems are notoriously hard to test.
It is common to hear stories of subtle bugs surfacing in well-architected,
heavily tested systems that have been running reliably in production
for years. The Jepsen testing suite, for instance,
routinely exposes critical consistency violations
and split-brain scenarios in established, battle-tested databases.

If we have robust CI/CD pipelines, extensive test coverage, and
strict code reviews, why is it so difficult to catch these bugs
before they hit production? The answer lies in the fundamental
mismatch between how we test software and
the reality of the environments in which distributed systems operate.

Unit tests validate local logic in isolation. Integration tests validate interactions between components.
But neither proves what clients observe when part of the system fails while requests are in flight.
End-to-end scenarios test the system with all components integrated,
but the focus is mostly on verifying functionality and sticking to the happy path.
When standard integration tests do simulate failures, they usually test clean, anticipated scenarios—like
gracefully shutting down a database node.
But in a distributed architecture, the hardest bugs do not live inside the isolated components;
they live in the unpredictable interactions between the components and
the infrastructure where partial failures and live traffic overlap.

When the systems are distributed, our assumptions about perfect
environments collapse.
As the classic “Fallacies of Distributed Computing” warn us,
the network is not reliable, latency is never zero,
and topology constantly changes.
Distributed systems suffer from partial failures.
One part of the system crashes or hangs while the rest
of the system keeps running, leading to conflicting views of
the cluster state.

In production, components rarely fail cleanly. A node doesn't just cleanly disconnect; it operates erratically, introducing subtle anomalies.
The network doesn't cleanly partition into two isolated halves. Instead, it suffers from asymmetric routing, selectively drops a small percentage of packets,
or delays specific messages just long enough to trigger a timeout on one node
but not another.
A process does not necessarily crash. Instead, it experiences a
Stop-The-World Garbage Collection pause on the JVM,
or CPU throttling. The pause lasts just long enough to cause bad message interleavings, causing the node to miss a consensus heartbeat, only for it to wake
up seconds later completely unaware that it was ever paused.
A disk does not fail completely. Instead, it experiences
a localized latency spike—taking 500ms instead of 2ms
to sync a Write-Ahead Log (WAL)—or it silently corrupts
a few sectors without causing
a complete hardware failure.
These gray failures create the exact interleavings of events that cause robust systems to break. Standard testing simply cannot create these highly specific, degraded conditions on demand.
To force these hard to find failure modes to surface, the common technique used is to inject faults into running systems intentionally.
From Chaos Engineering to Correctness Checking

Chaos engineering tests whether a system stays available under fault.
It introduces disruptions—like terminating pods or disrupting network
traffic—while monitoring infrastructure health. Consider a three-node
key-value store—Athens, Byzantium, and Cyrene—where reads and writes
require a majority of two replicas. If we kill a node during a quorum
write, the primary question chaos engineering asks is: does the write
still succeed and does the cluster recover?

Figure 1:
Chaos engineering focuses on resilience: does the system stay
available when a node is killed?

But availability is not the same as correctness. A system can
restart pods, keep serving traffic, and stay within latency limits
while still violating the semantics the client depends on. Returning
a successful response with stale or corrupted data means the system
is technically available, yet incorrect from the user's perspective.
Suppose a network partition isolates Cyrene while Alice writes a new
value. Athens and Byzantium form a majority, so the write succeeds,
leaving Cyrene on the old value:

Figure 2:
A quorum write succeeds on Athens and Byzantium while a network
partition leaves Cyrene holding the older value.

If Bob then reads from Cyrene, and it reads from its local state
instead of performing a quorum read,
Bob receives the older value even though Alice's write already
succeeded. Every request returned a response, so the system stayed
available, yet its consistency guarantee was broken:

Figure 3:
Bob reads from Cyrene and receives the stale value “Before Dawn”
even though Alice's write of “After Dawn” already succeeded.

Jepsen catches this by focusing strictly
on correctness from the client's perspective. It runs a live system,
injects faults, records the client-visible history of operations,
and checks whether that history is consistent with the system's
claimed semantics:

Alice: invoke set("title", "After Dawn")
Alice: ok     set("title", "After Dawn")
Bob:   invoke get("title")
Bob:   ok     get("title") -> "Before Dawn"   // violation: stale read after acknowledged write

This is the reason for faulting a live system. It allows
inspecting what happens to real client operations while the system has failures.

Chaos testing and frameworks like Jepsen are effective at finding bugs,
but finding a bug is only half the work. To fix a bug, you first need to
reproduce it. This is where live testing hits a wall. Reproducing a
failure in a live cluster fails on two separate levels:

Unseeded fault schedules: Faults are introduced randomly to mimic
unpredictable production conditions—dropping packets, crashing nodes, or
injecting delays. If this randomness is unseeded (or reseeded with the current
system time), every test run generates a completely different sequence of faults
at different times. A bug encountered on one run cannot be reproduced simply because
the test harness cannot regenerate that schedule. We can fix this to some extent by
using a seeded pseudo-random number generator, ensuring that rerunning with the same
seed produces the exact same sequence of fault decisions.

Execution nondeterminism: Even with the exact same sequence of faults,
the system is still not guaranteed to produce the same execution. In a live environment,
the application does not advance in lockstep with the fault generator. The software
runs against physical wall-clock time, asynchronous OS thread scheduling, and real
network and disk buffers. A microscopic timing shift—a garbage collection pause,
a thread context switch, or a delayed TCP ACK—changes which messages are in flight
at the exact millisecond a fault hits.

Consider a quorum write where one replica (Cyrene) is isolated by a network
fault. Athens, the coordinator, needs two of three replicas: its own write
and one acknowledgment. In Run 1, Byzantium's acknowledgment arrives early,
Athens forms a quorum, and Alice gets a success. In Run 2, with the exact
same fault injected, Byzantium's acknowledgment is delayed in transit.
Athens times out and returns a failure to Alice, and the acknowledgment
arrives only after the timeout has expired.

Neither outcome is wrong. But they are different executions of the same
test, and nothing in the test decides which one we get. If a bug lived
only on the Run 2 path, rerunning the test might land on Run 1 every time, missing the bug.

Figure 4:
Two runs with the same injected fault (Cyrene isolated) produce
different execution traces: in Run 1 the acknowledgment arrives in time,
while in Run 2 the coordinator times out before the delayed acknowledgment arrives.

There are four major sources of nondeterminism in a distributed
system: the system clock, thread scheduling, network timing, and
disk timing. Each changes when events become visible
to the software, producing different execution interleavings on
different runs.

Every timeout, retry and timestamp is a comparison against a
clock. In a live system, the time between two events depends on
everything else the machine is doing — a GC pause, a busy core, a
slow network hop — so the same operation can take 40ms in one run
and 120ms in the next. Wall clocks can also jump when NTP corrects
them. In the figure, the same write finishes inside the timeout
window in Run 1 and crosses it in Run 2. The code made the same
decision both times; the clock gave it a different answer. To
repeat a run, the test has to control what the clock reads.

Figure 5:
The same write operation can succeed or time out depending on how
much time passes before the acknowledgment arrives.

Within one process, the operating system decides which thread
runs next, and that decision changes with load, core count and
what else is running. Across a cluster it is worse: each process
runs at its own speed, and a process paused by GC falls behind the
others. In the figure, Alice's write and Bob's read arrive at
the same replica. In Run 1 the write handler runs first and Bob
sees the new value; in Run 2 the read handler runs first and Bob
sees the old one. To repeat a run, the test has to decide which
work runs next.

Figure 6:
Different thread scheduling orders produce different values for
the same read operation.

A message's delivery time depends on buffering, congestion,
retransmission and routing, none of which the program sees. Two
messages sent in one order can arrive in the other. In the figure,
the same replication message reaches the replica before Bob's read
in Run 1 and after it in Run 2, so Bob gets different values.
Injecting the same partition or loss rate does not fix this,
because the timing of every message that survives still varies. To
repeat a run, the test has to decide when each message is
delivered.

Figure 7:
The same replicated message becomes visible at different times
to a reader depending on network delivery timing.

A write returns once the bytes are in the OS page cache, not on
disk. They become durable when an fsync completes, or whenever the
kernel decides to flush them. How long that takes depends on the
device, its queue, and other I/O. In the figure, the coordinator
crashes at the same point in both runs. In Run 1 the flush had
finished and recovery finds “After Dawn”; in Run 2 it hadn't and
the value is gone. To repeat a run, the test has to decide when a
write becomes durable.

Figure 8:
The same coordinator crash leads to different recovery outcomes
depending on whether a write flush completed before the crash.

There are also sources inside the program itself, such as random
choices and the iteration order of its data structures. These are
handled by coding rules rather than by simulation, and we return
to them later.

Real systems advance because multiple subsystems keep progressing
through their own internal steps. The CPU executes instructions,
the NIC delivers packets, the disk completes flushes. These
progress mechanisms are hidden and not directly controlled by any
test.

Figure 9:
In a real system, CPU, NIC, and disk each progress at their own
pace. Software observes the resulting interleaving of events.

To repeat a run, the test must decide when the clock, the
processes, the network, and the disk make progress.
This is the core idea behind deterministic simulation testing.
Instead of running against real infrastructure, we run the entire cluster on a single
thread against a simulated clock, a simulated network, and a simulated
disk. Nothing progresses on its own. The test controls
when each component executes and delivers its work.

Figure 10:
In simulation, the test explicitly drives progress across the clock,
process, network, and disk (modeled in code as tick() calls).

Each source of nondeterminism from the previous section becomes
something the test controls:
Clock: it reads whatever the test has advanced it to.

Thread scheduling: the whole cluster runs on one thread,
and the test runs each process in a fixed order.

Network: a message is delivered only when the test
ticks the network.

Disk: a write becomes durable only when the test ticks
the disk.

Controlling progress this way makes it easy to simulate hard failures
like node crashes and network partitions. More importantly, it can
model routine slowdowns—a disk or network latency spike simply delays
completion by a few ticks. This makes gray failures, which are
otherwise extremely difficult to reproduce, straightforward to test.

Let's explore an example to see how this works in code. Using
Tickloom, a Java library for deterministic
simulation which I built
for teaching distributed systems,
we will see how distributed systems can be tested by simulating network
and storage.

The design of Tickloom draws heavily on
FoundationDB and
TigerBeetle. FoundationDB, an
open-source distributed transactional key-value store, pioneered
deterministic simulation testing for distributed databases using a
custom C++ coroutine language and deterministic scheduler. TigerBeetle,
a distributed financial transactions database, uses a clean,
single-threaded, tick-driven architecture and simulator that I found
easier to implement in Java. While the current Tickloom implementation
is based on callbacks and a custom future, it is also possible to
implement a custom deterministic scheduler using Java continuations,
which is planned for future work on Tickloom.

A distributed protocol implementation executes as a logical process.
A cluster is a set of these processes executing across one or more physical nodes.
Every process, in both testing and production,
runs on a single thread.
This design choice is the key, and the rest of the design, including
the network and file system interfaces, follows from it.

As we saw earlier, the operating system's thread scheduler is a source
of nondeterminism. To eliminate it, we explicitly drive execution
through a single-threaded main loop.
In production, this loop runs continuously in the main method.
In testing, it runs only until a specific condition is met or
a set duration is reached. The Process abstraction maintains its own internal task queue.
The main loop controls the execution by calling an explicit tick()
API on the process, controlling exactly when it is allowed to execute
its pending tasks, handle events, and make progress.

Every component whose progress needs to be controlled—whether a process, a network, or
a file system—implements one small interface:
Tickable. Calling tick() is how a component
makes progress: delivering messages, completing I/O, or running
pending tasks. The loop needs to know nothing about component
internals; it simply calls tick() on each in a fixed
order. Because components only advance when ticked, their state
never changes between ticks.

The main thread executing the tick calls must never block. In production, a node blocked
waiting for a reply would stop serving every other request.
To make sure single-threaded execution happens without blocking,
we do the following:
Network and storage calls are asynchronous.

Asynchronous APIs are modeled using a custom future that
allows standard composition but has no blocking get method and
strictly prevents the use of background threads.
No Thread.sleep() and no blocking calls.

Production network tasks use non-blocking Java NIO.
Blocking filesystem work that must run on a background thread
hands its results back to the node's main thread as events,
which are only processed during a tick.

To control when messages arrive, we should be able to swap the network implementation with a simulated one.
The protocol code must not notice the difference: the
same code has to run against the simulated network in a test
and against real sockets in production. So the core protocol logic never touches
sockets directly. It talks to the network only through an
interface, Network.
What travels over the network is a Message.

public record Message(
        ProcessId source,
        ProcessId destination,
        PeerType peerType,
        MessageType messageType,
        byte[] payload,
        String correlationId
)

It names its source and destination processes, its type, and
carries an encoded payload. The correlation ID maps a response to
the request.

The interface is asynchronous, because the process runs on a single
thread that must never block. send() hands a message
to the network and returns at once. It does not wait for the
message to be delivered, or for a reply. Messages arriving for
a particular process are delivered to the registered Process by calling
its onMessage() method. A reply is just another
message that arrives some ticks later. The network also has a
tick(), which drives its work.
There are two implementations of the Network interface:

In tests: SimulatedNetwork
passes messages directly between processes in memory.
This is the implementation that supports injecting faults like
network partitions, message loss and message delays.

In production: NioNetwork
implements the same non-blocking contract over real TCP sockets using
Java NIO and a single Selector. send() non-blockingly
enqueues encoded messages on a
NioConnection,
and the event loop flushes writes and dispatches incoming messages.

The simulated network has no sockets. It routes messages
directly to processes in memory, implementing the two contract methods.

It keeps track of NetworkLinks between pairs of processes and applies
configuration to these links in terms of delays, drop rates, and congestion:
The simulated network tracks partitions, packet drop rates, and delays across these links:

When a message is sent, the network checks the simulated link
between the sender and receiver. If the link is partitioned, or
matches a drop rule, the message is discarded.

A message that survives is not delivered immediately;
it is placed in a priority queue stamped with its delivery tick
(the next tick, or later if delayed or clogged) and an incrementing
sequence number to guarantee deterministic FIFO ordering.

Nothing in the queue moves until the network is ticked. On each
tick(), the network advances its virtual tick counter,
applies any dynamic fault changes, and delivers every message due for
the current tick.

Messages due at the same tick are delivered in the order they were sent.
Delivering a message simply calls deliver(message), which routes it to the
destination process's onMessage() method.

All communication in the cluster happens between processes, identified by
a ProcessId. In production, a process opens TCP sockets to
peers across the physical network. In simulation, however, every process
in the cluster—servers and clients alike—shares a single
SimulatedNetwork instance in memory. The network routes
messages by maintaining an internal registry of active processes: when a
process initializes, it registers its ProcessId, allowing the
network to dispatch incoming messages directly to that process's
onMessage() method. A message for an ID nobody registered is
logged and dropped.

A process is given its network when it is created. It never creates the
network itself, which is what lets a test hand it the simulated
one.

In its constructor, the process registers with the network, so
that messages addressed to its ID reach it, and then sets up its
message handlers.
Each implementation needs to handle different kinds of messages. A handler is an interface that allows providing a protocol specific implementation.

The QuorumReplica, for example, handles client requests and the
internal requests and responses between replicas:

The network calls onMessage, which runs the
handler for the message's type.

The handler runs to completion on the main thread. If it needs to
communicate with another process, it creates a message and sends it
through the network; the response arrives later as another message.

A timeout cannot be measured with a
time-of-day clock, because it is not guaranteed to be monotonic.
A common workaround is to
use monotonic clocks to measure elapsed time, but a process pause can
cause issues with this measurement. To make timeouts deterministic,
they are decoupled from any clock, and are based on a logical counter
representing elapsed time. A Timeout counts
ticks. A timeout of 10 expires after exactly
10 calls to tick().

To track in-flight requests and their timeouts without blocking,
processes use a
Request Waiting List.
The coordinator and the client register each request with its own
Timeout when it is added:

Figure 11:
When a request is added, the waiting list creates and starts a
tick-based Timeout.

On each tick, the waiting list advances the timeout counter and
checks whether it has expired.

Figure 12:
On each tick, the waiting list advances the timeout counter and
checks whether it has expired.
On the third tick the timeout has expired. So the associated request is expired with a TimeoutException:

Figure 13:
When a timeout expires, the waiting list removes the request
and throws a TimeoutException.

The QuorumReplica is the store from the earlier example. When a client sends a set
request, the replica that receives it acts as the coordinator. It
stamps the value with its clock and sends an internal set request
to all three replicas, including itself. It replies to the client
once a majority have acknowledged, and fails the write if no
majority answers before its request times out.

The earlier example had two runs of the same write with Cyrene
isolated. In Run 1 Byzantium's acknowledgment arrived in time;
in Run 2 it was delayed and the write timed out. In a live
cluster, nothing in the test decided which run we got. In the
simulation, the test decides.

A test builds a Cluster of quorum replicas on a simulated network, with a request timeout
of 10 ticks. It isolates Cyrene, and delays the link from
Byzantium to Athens by 20 ticks. Then Alice sends the write to
Athens, and the test ticks the cluster until the write is no
longer pending.

Cluster is a test utility that builds a cluster of given
processes—in this case QuorumReplica processes—and wires
them to the shared simulated network. It provides helper methods to
introduce faults (such as isolating processes and delaying links) as
well as to drive execution and verify assertions.

Instead of sleeping, tests call tickUntil to advance the cluster
until an expected condition holds.

Athens's own write is durable within a few ticks. Byzantium's
acknowledgment leaves Byzantium a few ticks later, and arrives 20
ticks after that. The timeout expires first, and the write fails. It
fails on every run. Set the delay to one tick and it succeeds on
every run.

Figure 14:
Run 2 in simulation: with Cyrene isolated and the link from
Byzantium delayed by 20 ticks, the 10-tick timeout fires before
the acknowledgment arrives, on every run.

The outcome now depends only on numbers the test chose: the
delay and the timeout. If a bug lived on the Run 2 path, this
test would hit it every time.

So far we discussed how to write tests for known fault interaction scenarios.
This is mostly useful for learning and teaching.
Production systems reveal bugs caused by interesting interleavings only after
they are up and running for a longer duration.
A common approach is to keep a system running for hours and introduce random failures.
This is a good practical way to explore the huge state space of all possible fault interactions.
Typically, a pseudorandom generator is used to decide when to inject a fault.
Making it seeded for every run, makes sure the run is repeatable.

Figure 15:
At each tick, the runner uses the seeded PRNG to decide whether to inject
a fault and pick which node to isolate.

The example implementation uses a common utility, a SimulationDecisions to have a central place,
where we make decisions. Whether to issue a client request or introduce
a fault are made by picking a value from random.nextDouble()
and comparing it with a configured probability threshold.
It also provides helper methods to pick fault types, select target
nodes, choose delay durations, and trigger periodic network healing:

The SimulationRunner initializes SimulationDecisions
with a random number generator with a seed.

protected final SimulationDecisions simulationDecisions; public SimulationRunner(long randomSeed, int clusterSize, int numClients, ProcessFactory processFactory, Cluster.ClientFactory clientFactory) throws IOException { Random random = new Random(randomSeed); this.simulationDecisions = new SimulationDecisions(random); this.cluster = Cluster.createSimulated(clusterSize, processFactory, random); this.clients = createClients(numClients, clientFactory); } private void runClusterFor(long runForTicks) { for (int i = 0; i < runForTicks; i++) { currentTick++; injectRandomFaults(); cluster.tick(); maybeIssueClientRequest(); } } private void maybeIssueClientRequest() { if (simulationDecisions.shouldIssueClientRequest()) { // A client is single-threaded and issues one request at a time. // If a request is pending, the request is buffered and issued later. SingleRequestIssuer client = simulationDecisions.pick(clients); client.issueRequest(); } }

The faults like isolate a random node, partition a random
pair, delay a random directed link, or drop all messages are then injected randomly.

The same seed produces the same sequence of faults, and the same
sequence of faults produces the same client visible results.
If a bug shows up for seed 42,
running seed 42 again reproduces it.

Alongside replaying with the seed, logging both the injected faults
(such as tick=12 isolate athens or
tick=23 delay athens->byzantium by 5) and the
process and network events at each tick makes failures much easier to
diagnose. Often, examining the combined fault schedule and execution
log is enough to spot the exact message interleaving that caused the
violation without even rerunning the simulation in a debugger—and
these structured, tick-stamped logs are particularly effective when
handed to an LLM to analyze what went wrong.

In production, every tick represents a fixed amount of real time. If
whoever invokes ticks has 10ms elapsed time between tick calls, a
timeout of 10 ticks expires after 100ms. Systems like
TigerBeetle
fix this interval to 10ms (tick_ms = 10), while etcd
typically uses a 100ms ticker with a 10-tick (one second) election
timeout.

A cluster under test has to run for the time duration it is testing. To
see a one-second timeout fire, a live test waits one real second.
Every delayed message, retry and recovery adds more. Fault testing
explores combinations of delays, faults and requests, and thousands
of possible runs quickly add up to days of real clock time.

The simulation advances tick by tick. So it does not need to wait
for real time to elapse.
The protocol still waits for 100
ticks, but those 100 ticks are 100 iterations of the
driver loop running the cluster.
Each iteration injects any faults for that tick, ticks the
cluster, and may issue a new client request. The loop runs as
fast as the CPU can execute it, so a run that would take hours
on a live cluster takes seconds.

Replay helps after a bug is found. Fast-forward helps find it in
the first place. Rare combinations of delays, failures, retries
and timeouts come up because the simulation can try so many
possible variations.

A common approach to check if the cluster behaved as expected, is to
produce a client-visible history:
the sequence of invocations and completions that clients
observed. This history can be fed into correctness checkers.

The approach used by
Jepsen is to record client operations and their results
in EDN format. Each client operation produces an :invoke
event, followed by an :ok, :fail, or
timeout:

After a run, the SimulationRunner passes the recorded
history to a ConsistencyChecker, which checks whether
it is linearizable for a register:

If the checker finds a violation, the seed that produced it
is enough to reproduce the exact execution. There is no need
to guess at timing or hope for the right interleaving. The
developer can step through the exact tick sequence that led
to the bug.

The storage layer can cause issues when crashes happen abruptly,
before data in the operating system's page cache and storage buffers
is durable. Operating systems provide separate APIs like
fsync to guarantee that data is persisted onto the
storage media, but there are tricky error
scenarios when an fsync call fails. This is one
reason many modern storage systems use O_DIRECT to
bypass the operating system's page cache and read and write directly
to the storage device. File system simulation can be implemented in a
way similar to the network: storage code talks to files through an
asynchronous interface, FileIO.

Every operation returns a future instead of blocking the main thread.
A completed write() only means the bytes are visible to
later reads. Only a completed sync() guarantees that
previous writes are durable across a crash.
There are two implementations of FileIO:

In tests: SimulatedFileIO operates on an
in-memory SimulatedFile and advances queued operations
on tick().

In production: SingleThreadedFileIO executes
FileChannel calls on a dedicated background I/O thread
and delivers completions back to the main thread during
tick().

The core difference between written data and durable data can simply be
represented by two byte arrays.
SimulatedFile represents a file as two byte arrays in
memory: visible holds bytes written so far including
unsynced writes, and durable holds bytes that have been
synced. Reads and writes use visible. Calling
sync() copies visible to
durable. A crash discards unsynced writes by resetting
visible back to durable, allowing storage
components like a Write-Ahead Log to be
tested deterministically across crashes and restarts.

Figure 16:
Writing updates visible; calling sync()
copies visible to durable.

Figure 17:
A crash before sync() resets visible back
to durable, losing unsynced writes.

To fulfill the async contract of FileIO,
SimulatedFileIO wraps SimulatedIO.
Operations like
read() and write() submit their work to a
queue and return a future:

An explicit tick() call executes the queued operations on
SimulatedFile and completes their futures:

One thing to notice is the use of custom Future implementation in this API.
It is convenient to have a Future abstraction for composing async
operations. But standard futures like Java's
CompletableFuture are risky in a single-threaded event
loop for two reasons. Blocking methods like get() or
join() would freeze the main thread and prevent the tick
loop from ever completing the operation. And asynchronous combinators
like thenApplyAsync() dispatch callbacks onto background
thread pools, reintroducing thread-scheduling nondeterminism and race
conditions on replica state.

TickCompletableFuture
avoids both by not exposing any blocking calls. It has no background
executors and allows attaching callbacks to compose async operations.

Deterministic simulation testing cannot be added as an afterthought;
it requires upfront architectural investment. As the need for a custom
future illustrates, high-level design choices—a single-threaded core,
asynchronous I/O interfaces, and avoiding thread-heavy libraries—are
critical and have to be built into the system from the start.

Crucially, these constraints apply only on the deterministic side of an
architectural seam. Interfaces like Network,
FileSystem, FileIO, and Clock
form the boundary between the simulated core and the operating system.
Behind that seam, production implementations such as
NioNetwork,
SingleThreadedFileIO,
and SystemClock are free to use background I/O threads,
ExecutorService, NIO socket channels, and system clocks—as
long as they deliver their results back onto the single-threaded
tick() loop.

To keep the core deterministic and the seam intact, the code must
follow six strict coding rules:

No system clock calls:
Time must come from the simulated Clock or tick counter.
Nothing like System.currentTimeMillis(),
System.nanoTime(), or Instant.now()
can be directly used.

No unseeded randomness:
All random decisions or IDs should come from the provided
seeded RandomGenerator or IdGen.

No threads or standard futures:
The code should not directly use Thread,
Executor, or CompletableFuture.

No direct network or disk I/O:
All I/O must go through the Network and FileIO
interfaces.

No iteration over unordered collections:
While key lookups on a HashMap or Map.of() are deterministic,
iterating over HashMap, HashSet, or
ConcurrentHashMap (for example, when
RequestWaitingList scans pending requests to expire
timeouts) can visit entries in a different order across runs. To
prevent accidental iteration over these unordered collections, core state uses
LinkedHashMap and LinkedHashSet, which
guarantee insertion-order iteration.

No cross-thread callbacks across the seam: Background threads
in production adapters must never directly invoke methods or
complete futures on the deterministic side. In
IOThread,
for example, the disk thread never calls
future.complete() itself—doing so would execute storage
and replica callbacks on the I/O thread, introducing data races in
production that never happen in simulation. Instead, it queues
completions for the main thread to drain during tick().

Because even a single usage of HashMap or
System.currentTimeMillis() inside a message handler will
silently break the replayability guarantee
when a rare fault sequence hits that code path later—relying on developer
discipline or code reviews to enforce these rules does not scale.
Instead, we can guard the system using automated
architectural fitness functions:

Static fitness functions with ArchUnit: Using a tool like
ArchUnit, a
DeterminismRulesTest
suite runs on every build as an atomic, static fitness function to
verify that core protocol and storage packages stay behind the
architectural seam and obey the first five determinism rules.

A holistic fitness function for distributed correctness: Once
the static rules and runtime thread checks guarantee deterministic
execution, the seeded FaultInjectingSimulationRunner
and ConsistencyChecker act as a holistic fitness
function that verifies system-wide invariants like linearizability
and crash durability across numerous fault sequences.

A natural question is whether designing for single-threaded simulation
hurts production performance or resource usage. In practice, the
opposite is often true. Most of the distributed systems are often IO bound.
So single-threaded processing with
asynchronous, batched I/O actually works better, eliminating locking and thread
context-switching. This is the same architecture used for high
throughput and low latency systems like Redis,
FoundationDB, and TigerBeetle.

The trade-off is that handlers on the tick()
thread must never block or perform long-running CPU work, which would
stall message processing. Because a single event
loop uses one CPU core for protocol logic, scaling across a multi-core
machine is done by running multiple independent processes rather than sharing mutable state across
a large thread pool.

In my experience, while building the simulation foundation takes
upfront effort, it makes the core protocol logic easier to write and
evolve. Separating the core from network sockets, threads, and clock
time makes it easier to reason about. As seen in
QuorumReplica, the handlers are plain single-threaded
code.

The biggest benefit is the convenience of exploring random fault
combinations. Evolving the system becomes much safer and easier, as
the fault scenario tests act as a fitness function.
Learning and the Use of LLMs

An excellent side effect is using this technique for learning and
teaching distributed systems. Once foundational code like Tickloom is
in place, those abstractions provide a harness
that allows using LLMs as a natural-language interface
to build and explore systems.

While reading a book, documentation, or an engineering article, we
often need to work through tricky corner-case scenarios that are
usually only sketched as diagrams on a whiteboard. With a
deterministic simulation harness in place, we can ask an LLM to
generate executable scenario tests and explore working code directly.
For example, while reading the quorum linearizability anomaly in
Designing Data-Intensive Applications,
an LLM can translate the book's diagram directly into an executable
Tickloom scenario like
DDIA_LinearizabilityScenarioTest,
where link delays and partitions cause one client to read a new value
and a subsequent client to read a stale one. It becomes much easier to
deep-dive and learn with this kind of executable codebase to explore.
